# Preface {.unnumbered #sec-preface}

```{=html}
<span id="placing-profiles-in-a-unified-theory-book" class="legacy-anchor" aria-hidden="true"></span>
```

```{=html}
<span id="sec-research-questions" class="legacy-anchor" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span id="sec-p2-home" class="legacy-anchor" aria-hidden="true"></span>
```

Public agencies and research organizations routinely compare schools, districts, neighborhoods and other institutions using several indicators. These comparisons may determine which units receive closer attention, how performance is communicated, or where further investigation begins. Yet the quantities of interest are seldom known precisely, and the indicators need not support the same ordering. A district may have greater economic need than another while having fewer barriers to educational access. Even when the substantive priorities are agreed, the evidence may support some comparisons more strongly than others.

This book concerns the choice of comparisons to communicate under these circumstances. We treat a report as a statistical decision, with consequences both for issuing an erroneous direction and for withholding a useful one. A common grade places the units in one ordered grouping. A domain profile assigns a separate grade in each domain, allowing priorities to cross between domains. In either form, different grades communicate a direction, while a shared grade withholds it. Sharing a grade therefore leaves the comparison unresolved; it does not establish equality of the underlying quantities.

Our aim is to develop these two reporting families within a common set of definitions and to relate them to the literatures on Bayesian ranking, measurement, multicriteria decision analysis and selective reporting. These literatures address overlapping questions from different starting points. Ranking methods study uncertainty about relative position; measurement determines what the indicators represent; multicriteria analysis examines the role of values and trade-offs; selective reporting considers when a conclusion should be withheld. Bringing these questions together helps us specify what a report is intended to say and assess how well it does so.

Several distinctions recur throughout the book. Combining indicator magnitudes into a single target differs from assigning importance to directional errors on separate criteria. More precise estimates can reduce uncertainty without resolving a substantive conflict between criteria. Likewise, a report with more grades communicates more detail, but the number of grades alone does not determine how many comparisons it makes. The formal development gives these distinctions mathematical expression. Small examples show why they matter before the more general results are introduced.

The methods take a probability law for the quantities of interest as an input. In an application this may be a posterior distribution obtained from a statistical model; in an exact example it may be a finite distribution specified directly. We examine how that information, together with reporting costs and restrictions, determines the choice of report. This makes the book useful both for constructing a reporting procedure and for examining an existing one: which directions does it assert, how are errors valued, and which comparisons remain unreported? A report supplies information for policy; choosing an allocation or intervention also requires an explicit institutional objective.

## Organization and readership {#sec-preface-organization}

We have written for researchers, graduate students and analysts concerned with comparative reporting, particularly in education and public policy. Familiarity with probability, conditional expectation and statistical inference will be helpful. Knowledge of Bayesian modeling is useful for the applications, although the reporting problem can first be understood through the finite examples. The methodological chapters use mathematical notation to state assumptions precisely, while the applications and figures give more concrete interpretations. Longer arguments are collected in the appendices.

The opening parts establish the public reporting problem and review its intellectual foundations. We then introduce the shared definitions and develop common grades, before allowing the grade columns to differ across domains. This progression makes it possible to examine which results carry over and which require additional information. For example, additive expected loss can use domain marginals, whereas protection against a joint error event can depend on how the domains vary together. Whether the optimization itself separates also depends on the restrictions imposed on the reports.

The computing and evaluation chapters examine how reports are obtained and compared. They distinguish uncertainty about the targets from numerical approximation and from the limits of an optimization search. They also distinguish performance under the law used to select a report from performance under another law or across repeated datasets. The application chapters return to the substantive questions that motivate these distinctions. Studies of Alabama economic need, geographic priorities in the Opportunity Atlas, PISA comparisons and California accountability illustrate common-grade or separate scalar analyses. Exact examples and a fictional forty-site study develop the domain-profile ideas. The final chapters consider institutional interpretation and the questions that remain for further research.

## Reading routes {#sec-reading-routes}

```{=html}
<span id="for-an-applied-reader" class="legacy-anchor" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span id="for-a-mathematical-reader" class="legacy-anchor" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span id="for-a-p1-reader-checking-a-claim" class="legacy-anchor" aria-hidden="true"></span>
```

Readers developing a reporting method can begin with the [shared definitions](chapters/09-targets-actions-laws.qmd), continue through common grades and [domain profiles](chapters/14-profile-actions.qmd), and then study computation and [numerical uncertainty](chapters/21-numerical-uncertainty.qmd). The [proof appendix](appendices/A-proofs.qmd) gives the formal arguments, and the [notation guide](appendices/B-notation.qmd) collects the decision objects and probability statements. Reading the small examples alongside a derivation is often helpful: they expose the role of a restriction or dependence assumption with relatively little notation.

Readers beginning with an application can start with the [exact examples](chapters/25-worked-examples.qmd), [Alabama economic need](chapters/27-alabama-need.qmd), [Opportunity Atlas](chapters/28-opportunity-atlas.qmd), [PISA comparisons](chapters/29-pisa-comparisons.qmd), or [California accountability](chapters/30-cde-accountability.qmd). Each case states its comparison population, target, uncertainty representation and permitted report. The [forty-site illustration](chapters/31-synthetic-need.qmd) shows how the same units can receive different grades across domains. References within these chapters lead back to the relevant definitions and forward to [institutional interpretation](chapters/32-governance-communication.qmd). A course or reading group can use the same route, pairing a substantive case with the methodological chapters needed to understand it.

The online format provides further opportunities to examine the ideas. Supplementary Boxes link to postrank Explorer applications and suggest comparisons to try; screenshots introduce the displays before readers open an application. Some Boxes illustrate the argument at hand, while others introduce related concepts in uncertainty, measurement or decision making. The book also contains interactive examples with fixed tables and accompanying explanations, so the central argument can be followed without using the controls.

The postrank software and the [reproduction appendix](appendices/E-reproduction.qmd) connect the definitions to computational practice. Executable material appears in the computing chapters and supplementary materials, where input preparation and numerical assessment can be treated in detail. The theory chapters concentrate on the reporting decision and its assumptions. Readers can therefore move between a mathematical result, a worked comparison and its implementation as their questions require.
